# 18-careforce — sources

Back-test entry `18-careforce.yaml`: Careforce, AI agents that call and book the patients a health center never reaches
(YC Fall 2024). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only, read that day. Quotes are verbatim from the page named.
"Author's choice" marks the smallest plausible choice made where the public material is silent. The launch era is the
Launch YC post of 2024-11-22 and the weeks around it (the founder's gap-11 rule: every figure pinned to the launch era
where one exists; anything later is marked as later, and a later price sits under *Status today*).

Main sources (short names used below):
- [LYC] Launch YC: "Careforce - Must-have AI agents for Healthcare admin", 2024-11-22 (created_at in the page data) — https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/MJj-careforce-must-have-ai-agents-for-healthcare-admin

- [CHCF] California Health Care Foundation investment page (CHCF is an investor, $500,000, February 2026; the page blocks direct fetches, so the quote is as the diversity research recorded it) — https://www.chcf.org/investment/careforce/

## The eight founder-emulation items

1. **Who.** Medical assistants at community health centers, who work the outreach lists between patients.
   [LYC] "For health centers & practices this means MAs (short-staffed with front desk and intake) end up spending most
   of their time on admin tasks and most patients are never outreached & scheduled for vital screenings/visits,
   leaving a 1/3rd of care unserviced." → `roles[assistant]`, `context.actor`, `actor_plural`. Author's choice: of
   [LYC]'s three segments (health centers and practices; digital health and CCM companies; payers) the first, the one
   the post describes by its staff.

2. **What (the job).** Get every patient due for a screening or visit called and booked.
   [LYC] "Most care coordination & data sharing is still manually done by staff through phones, email, fax because of
   unintegrated systems and custom workflows too unique to automate out of the box." → `statements.problem`,
   `context.job`, `interpretations.problem`.

3. **When / where.** Each working day, when the list of due patients has to be called between patients.
   [LYC] "Outreach using 50+ editable scripts (mammograms, pre-post-op, onboarding etc.)"; "Leave Voicemails, Sending
   reminders, and autonomously retry patients as needed". → `context.circumstance`, `occasion: outreach call list`.
   Author's choice: the window {5, WORKING_DAYS} (spec 120: a daily rhythm in a clinic read as working days) and
   Frequency 3 to 5 working days out of 5; [LYC] gives no count. Prevalence `p_80_100` follows from "most patients are
   never outreached".

4. **Which people.** US community health centers (FQHCs) and primary-care practices that work outreach lists by phone.
   [LYC] "Our AI agents are already Live with health centers and digital health companies helping analyze, call,
   schedule, and generate revenue." → `context.segment`, `market: US` (a San Francisco company, [KFF]).

5. **Who pays.** The health center. [LYC] "Let us take on your calling, coordination, and manual admin work so you can
   get more patients in the door without burning out your staff."; "increase revenue with Careforce AI Agents".
   → `persona.decision_maker: {role: director}`. Author's choice: the decider is the health center's executive or
   operations director and the tested role "The CFO" (a second role, "The board", listed: FQHCs are governed by
   boards). Purchase friction's three items (a HIPAA security review — tested; giving the agent access to the EMR; a
   board vote) are the author's, from [LYC]'s "Use EMR, Scheduling, payer and provider portals through UI or API
   Integrations" and [KFF]'s note that plans "are responsible for ensuring that technology complies with state and
   federal regulations, including patient privacy and data security". Commitment's step, "try it on one outreach list":
   [LYC] "We'd love to learn about your use cases and give you personalized demos unique to your use case."; the
   wording is the author's.

6. **Mechanism.** Two agents: one calls, texts, emails and books; one pulls data and builds the lists.
   [LYC] "Careforce creates autonomous agents that are able to take on these human-glue tasks and complete them in the
   same way as your staff would without the need for integrations." [LYC] (Angelica) "Call, text, email, and schedule
   patients autonomously"; "Speak in 29 Languages to engage and educate across demographics"; "Make 100 calls / min.
   and finish a year's worth of outreach in weeks". [LYC] (David) "Prepare reports, and generate lists for Angelica to
   realize the unrealized revenue". → `statements.solution`, `solution_mechanism`; Compatibility (the list straight out
   of the EMR — tested; open slots; patients picking up unknown numbers) and Adoption friction (hand the day's list to
   an AI caller — tested; take the calls it hands back, from [KFF] "This will always be, in my opinion, an AI-human
   combination"). Relative advantage's two benefits are [LYC]'s retries (fewer_attempts) and "finish a year's worth
   of outreach in weeks" (shorter_time); the wording is the author's.

7. **Price and cost.** No price is public at launch or today: [LYC] offers demos, [WB] has no pricing page near launch,
   [SITE] has none today. The founder's price, AMOUNT_PERIOD **$1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month**, is the
   operator's reading: a monthly per-site fee of the size community health centers pay for a part-time outreach caller's
   share of work (an MA's hour is about $22, [BLS]; $1,500 to $3,000 is roughly 70 to 135 such hours), set below what
   the bookings it claims to recover would bring in. It is said in `statements.commercial` as the founder would type
   it, and marked there and in the header as the operator's.
   Existing sacrifice, RATE about **30% to 33%** of the patients due for a visit or screening per health center a month,
   lost as "Visits and screenings never booked because nobody reached the patient": [LYC]'s "1/3rd of care unserviced"
   for health centers (33%) and "costing 30% in bookings" across healthcare (30%). Ability to pay is read `budget` by
   the engine (a percent of patients never compares with an amount a month), so the directors answer the budget item.

8. **Occasions.** The stories are scripted from [LYC]'s scripts list (mammograms, pre-post-op), the short-staffing it
   names, and [KFF]; no respondent is a real person. [KFF] (Kern's CEO) "But we are already stretched thin. We need this
   functionality to be much more effective and augment our efforts." [KFF] "In samples of actual conversations provided
   to a reporter, Angelica sounded lifelike at first, although more than once cross-talk with a patient caused the
   program to pause suddenly."

## Respondents → the public account each is based on

Medical assistants (PRIMARY link, Parts 1 and 2):
- Yesenia Morales → [LYC] "short-staffed with front desk and intake"; the mammogram script from [LYC]'s scripts list.
- Thanh Nguyen → [LYC] "Speak in 29 Languages"; [KFF] a member who valued being called in Spanish; an MA who calls the Vietnamese-speaking patients herself is the author's.
- Keisha Robinson → [LYC] "most patients are never outreached & scheduled"; two staff out is the author's.
- Olga Petrenko → author's invention, filling a gap: a practice with a dedicated outreach coordinator whose list gets done, so the problem is not a chorus (against on Importance).
- Marisol Vega → author's invention: a chipped (rather_not_say) story, GUESSED by code.
- Darnell Hayes → author's invention: a vague, habitual story with no one occasion (GUESSED).
- Fatima Al-Sayed, Brandon Kealoha → author's invention: gate No (no outreach list worked in the window).
- Rosa Jimenez → [KFF] "it took her a minute before she realized she wasn't speaking with a human" and the cross-talk pauses, turned sceptical: older patients who hang up on a recording (Relative advantage negative).
- Abena Owusu → [LYC] "unintegrated systems" and [LYC] (David) "Use UI to download data across EMRs & portals"; a list built by hand fails the tested condition (Compatibility no).
- Priyanka Shah → author's invention, filling a gap: bookings into blocked slots, so she would not hand the list over (Adoption friction probably not).
- Miguel Ferreira → [LYC] "care coordination" staff; a care coordinator works the list (the Current-solution escape, someone_else_checks).

Health center directors (COMMERCIAL_B2B link, Part 3 only; no story by rule). Their picks are the author's, shaped by:
- Linda Okafor-Reyes, Harold Jensen → [LYC] "increase revenue" and "book 30% more appointments": directors who pay at the founder's band.
- Samuel Goldberg → author's invention: would pay above the band but tests first.
- Carmen Ruiz → author's invention: pays below the band until bookings are shown.
- Aisha Bello → author's invention, filling a gap: a health center booked out for weeks, so unbooked patients cost it nothing it counts (Nothing; would not pay).
- Richard Lam → [KFF] the privacy and data-security duty; a director who cannot say the cost or the price (both escapes).
- Nadia Haddad → [KFF] "an AI-human combination"; a pilot with staff listening in.
- Joseph Whitecloud → author's invention: outreach paid from grant money (taken from other spend), below the band.

The split on Price (4 of the 7 who name a rung at $1,500 or above) is the author's: no public account gives what a
health center would pay. No respondent carries the name of a customer, patient, official or founder in the sources.

## Status today

Same idea, traction moved to health plans. [SITE] still sells the two agents for payors, plans, FQHCs and specialties.
The public customers are Medi-Cal health plans doing renewal outreach: [KFF] "Kern Family has spent about $370,000 on the
software by Careforce, a San Francisco startup, to facilitate rapid and repeated outreach to members when it's time to
renew their coverage."; "estimated it would have had to spend $2.4 million in staffing costs to match the program's more
than 800,000 calls to its 387,000 members"; "Kern Family's Medi-Cal renewal rate in April was 94.9%". [CHCF] "With the
aid of Careforce, KFHC renewed 96% of their members during the first year, compared to 38% before using the AI platform."
[KFF] says the agent "speaks more than 30 languages" (29 at launch). Price today: not public.

## Could not be sourced

- **A price, at any time.** The founder's $1,500 to $3,000 per health center a month is the operator's reading (item 7);
  the only public money figure is one health plan's cumulative spend ([KFF], 2026), not a unit price.
- **A health center's share of patients never booked, measured.** The 30% to 33% are the founders' own launch claims
  (one for health centers, one for healthcare overall), not a study.
- **A buyer title.** [LYC] asks "Healthcare Orgs" for demos; the director as decider, the CFO and the board as the roles,
  and the three Purchase friction items are the author's.
- **First-person MA accounts.** None public; the occasions are scripted from [LYC] and [KFF] (a health plan, not a
  health center).
- **A launch-era site.** [WB] holds no snapshot between 2024-05-18 and 2025-11-13; the launch post is the only
  launch-era page. [CHCF] could not be fetched directly (a bot check); its quote is as the diversity research read it.
- An MA's hour: [BLS]'s median stands in; no cost in the entry is in hours.

screens.why5: My agent retries patients autonomously, so the point is that staff don't have to keep calling back; 'without calling back again and again' blurs who stops calling, and 'a year's worth of outreach in weeks' became 'same day', which fits a daily list but is not quite what I said.
screens.instead: Rows: More patients on the list booked into a visit · You don't have to keep calling the same patients back · The whole day's list called, not just part of it · Patients called in their own language

screens.why1: After I've said how it fits their work and what it does better, asking what my MAs must do to start is the natural last solution question before price.
screens.why2: 'What will they have to do to start using it?' with a hint about setup and learning is plain to me as a founder selling into health centers.
screens.why3: I know exactly what onboarding asks of an MA: hand over the day's outreach list and take back the calls Angelica can't close, so I can answer this from my own work.
screens.why4: The only option is the escape 'Leave this out of the study', which fits a free-text screen, and nothing is missing.
screens.why5: Keel's belief 'Most would hand the day's list to an AI caller' keeps my first step word for word; my second step, taking the hand-backs, stays as a listed item rather than the tested one, which is what I meant.

screens.why1: Right after I said what MAs must do to start, Keel shows the steps it drew from my answer, and these are the two I meant: hand the list over, and take back what it can't close.
screens.why2: Every word is plain to an MA (the day's list, AI caller, calls), though the screen says 'AI caller' in one row and 'the agent' in the next.
screens.why3: Handing off the outreach list and picking up the patients who need a human are things an MA does or would do on a working day.
screens.why4: The two rows are distinct and in my words, but 'AI caller' and 'agent' name the same thing two ways, and a likely step is missing: checking the bookings it puts into the schedule.
screens.why5: It keeps what I typed: hand over the day's list (the tested one) and take the calls it hands back, with nothing of Careforce's names (Angelica, David) leaking.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Hand the day's list to an AI caller' / 'Take the calls the AI caller hands back' / 'Check the bookings it puts in the schedule'

screens.why1: Right after choosing who asks, it makes sense to choose how medical assistants answer, and as a founder I'd want them answering between patients in a busy clinic.
screens.why2: The choice is clear, but 'Daphne Daphne' reads as a typo and 'Still recording · ready in a few minutes' makes me read twice to tell whether that's Daphne's status or something about my study.
screens.why3: I know MAs grab a minute at the front desk or in a loud hallway, so I can judge from my own clinics whether they'd tap or talk.
screens.why4: AI voice, read-and-tap, or let them pick covers the real choices without overlap, and the loud-room accuracy note speaks to exactly what a clinic floor is like.
screens.why5: It keeps 'medical assistants' as I typed it, and nothing about Careforce, Angelica or the directors leaks into how the respondent answers.
screens.instead: How should medical assistants answer? — Daphne asks each question aloud and on screen; they talk, type or tap (ready in a few minutes) / They read each question and tap; boxes take voice or typing (ready now) / Offer both and let each one pick when they open the link

screens.why1: Once the study is built and I've chosen how MAs will answer, the obvious last step is deciding who gets the link, and I can send it to the MAs at the health centers we already work with.
screens.why2: Plain founder language: a personal link per named person, a list from Keel's search, or one open link posted to a group are all clear on first read.
screens.why3: I know which MAs and outreach staff I can reach by name through our live health center customers, so I can answer this from what I actually do.
screens.why4: The three ways in (named contacts, a Keel search list, an open group link) are distinct and cover how I'd reach MAs; the Google sign-in on the open link is a minor snag for clinic staff on work accounts but doesn't break the choice.
screens.why5: Nothing about Careforce's agents, price or roles is on this screen, and my pick, people I know by name, is kept as I made it.

screens.why_b1: The status 'Too few to call' sits beside '4 answered · 5 needed to call it' on every card, but the header says 7 people answered and never says why only 4 count, so the deciding number is not cleanly tied to the verdict.
screens.why_b2: The bar (5 needed) and the count (4) are plain, but '3 too few · 7 people answered' against '4 answered' on each card takes a second look to work out who was counted.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility, Relative advantage and Adoption friction carry exactly the belief lines I checked on the way in, though the solution statement above them is garbled ('the medical assistant one AI agent calls…').
screens.why_b4: Nothing tells me what to do: not whether to send the study to more medical assistants, how many more, or why 3 of my 7 dropped out of every card.
screens.why_b5: It refuses to call any belief on 4 answers and shows n on every card, so it claims nothing the data cannot carry.
screens.instead: Your 3 solution beliefs can't be called yet: of 7 who answered, only 4 worked an outreach list in the last 5 working days (the other 3 didn't). Get at least 1 more MA who did, and each belief can be called.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside a number, but the status line says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', so I have to work out that it means 4 counted, and it never says the 3-of-4 lean is on the held side.
screens.why_b2: Better 3 and Same 1 over 4 are plain, but the bar reads '3 of 4 (no more than 1 in 3 say no difference or worse)', which mixes a for-count with an against-rule, and I had to check that 1 of 4 clears it.
screens.why_b3: Relative advantage and 'patients reached without calling back again and again' are word for word the belief I checked.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is generic; it does not tell me that one more counted MA settles it, or that the only no comes from a center that already has a coordinator clearing the list.
screens.why_b5: n stays visible, Darnell's guess is set aside, and the small group is called 'a lean, not a call'; nothing claims more than 3 of 4 can carry.
screens.instead: Leans held but too few to call: 3 of 4 counted MAs say a lot better. The one no is Olga, whose coordinator already gets through the list. One more counted answer settles it, so send the study to one more MA at a short-staffed center.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Too few to call' sits beside its deciding number, and the So line ties them plainly: 4 counted, 5 needed.
screens.why_b2: The chart's four answer bars and the strip's 4 for and 1 ghost read at once, but the bar '3 of 4 (no more than 1 in 3 say probably not or no)' frames a count for me and a share against me together, so it takes a second look.
screens.why_b3: Adoption friction and 'Most would hand the day's list to an AI caller' are exactly what I checked on the way in.
screens.why_b4: 'Nothing is settled here yet' is a generic line: it doesn't say that all four counted would hand the list over, two only if it was clearly worth it, or that one more clear answer would let it be called.
screens.why_b5: The header says '4 answered' while the count line says '5 answered · 4 counted', a small misstatement of n, though 'a lean, not a call' rightly keeps the result from being oversold.
screens.instead: 4 of 5 counted, all would hand over the day's list (2 only if it was clearly worth it); one more clear answer and this can be called, so find out what 'clearly worth it' means to them.

screens.why_b1: Each box opens on "Too few to call" with "4 answered · 5 needed to call it" right beside it, so I know there's no verdict yet and exactly why.
screens.why_b3: Compatibility and Relative advantage are named as I checked them, and both belief lines are word for word what I confirmed on the way in.
screens.why_b4: Nothing says what two of four saying their list doesn't come out of the EMR means for Angelica, or for leading with David to build the list; Adoption friction's absence isn't explained either.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible on every box and the low n is named as too few to call; the against counts and the one MA who never saw the question (Thanh) are stated plainly, with no claim past them.
screens.why_b6: The quotes add what I didn't type: at some centers the list is a manager's printed spreadsheet or a hand-filled clipboard, so the EMR isn't the source. A practice with a coordinator is buried by prior auths and rooming, not outreach.
screens.instead: Too few to call yet, but 2 of the 4 who answered say their list doesn't come out of the EMR: a manager's spreadsheet or a clipboard. Test whether David building the list is the first sell before Angelica calls it, and get one more answer to call Compatibility.

screens.why1: Right after I said whether I got through my whole call list this week, it makes sense to show me something that would do those calls for me.
screens.why2: EMR, outreach list and payer portals are my everyday words, but "without an integration project" is IT talk I wouldn't use, and "patients booked by AI agents" doesn't tell me plainly what the thing is.
screens.why3: Calling, texting, retrying no-answers and booking into the schedule is exactly what I do between rooming patients, so I can picture it against my own day.
screens.why4: It is a card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It is clearly an idea shown on purpose and keeps the founder's points (calls, texts and emails in 29 languages, retries, books in the EMR, builds the due lists), with nothing slipping in where it shouldn't.
screens.why6: Heard once it's a long run of six sentences about two agents, the opening "patients booked by AI agents" is awkward said aloud, and "integration project" is a mouthful at the end, so it's hard to hold in one hearing.
screens.instead: Imagine Careforce, an AI that calls your due-for-care list for you. It calls, texts and emails each patient in their language, tries again when they don't pick up, and books them in your schedule. It also builds the list of who is due from your EMR and the insurance portals. The people building it believe it would call patients the way you would, without IT having to set anything up.

screens.why1: Right after the card about AI agents booking patients, it makes sense to ask whether my call list already sits in the EMR, since that's where anything like that would have to pull from.
screens.why2: Outreach list and EMR are words I use every day, and 'straight out of' is how I'd say it myself.
screens.why3: I work these lists between patients, so I know whether I ran the report in the EMR myself or got a spreadsheet from the payer or the care coordinator.
screens.why4: 'Yes, with some steps' sits awkwardly against 'straight out of,' since a list that took steps wasn't straight out, and 'No' lumps a payer gap list together with one I built by hand.
screens.why5: The idea card is shown on purpose, and the question itself uses my words, not the company's, so nothing leaks beyond the card.
screens.why6: It's one short question with three short options and the escape said last, so it's easy to hold on one hearing.
screens.instead: Think of your last outreach list. Did it come out of the EMR? Yes, I ran it myself; yes, but I had to clean it up; no, it came from the payer or a registry; or no, we built it by hand. Or say you can't tell.

screens.why1: I just said my list didn't come straight out of the EMR, so asking what happened instead is the obvious next thing.
screens.why2: EMR and outreach list are my words, but 'You said no to this: the list came straight out of the EMR' is a clumsy echo I'd have to read twice to follow.
screens.why3: I can say where my list actually comes from, like the payer gap report or what my supervisor hands me, but why it isn't pulled from the EMR is usually the quality person's call, so I'd partly be guessing.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in, with no options.
screens.why5: 'What got in the way' assumes the EMR should be the source and something blocked it, when for me the list just comes from somewhere else, so it leans toward the founder's view.
screens.why6: The colon and the backwards restatement sound stiff out loud, though it's still one short question I could answer.
screens.instead: Where did your last outreach list come from, if not straight out of the EMR?

screens.why1: Right after the idea card and the question about where my list comes from, asking whether this would have helped with my last list is the natural next question.
screens.why2: I get it, but 'go better' is fuzzy (faster calls, more patients booked, less work between rooming?) and I'd have to pick what it means for myself.
screens.why3: I know my last list well, but I've only seen one line about Careforce, so how much better it would have been is partly a guess.
screens.why4: A lot better, a little better, no difference, worse covers it without overlap, and 'I can't tell' is the honest out when all I've seen is one line about it.
screens.why5: The card says plainly what is being shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms comes through in the question.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I can hold after one hearing, with one escape said last.
screens.instead: Would Careforce have gotten more of your last outreach list booked, or not? A lot more · A few more · About the same · Fewer · I can't tell

screens.why1: After asking whether Careforce would have helped with my last list, it makes sense to ask whether I'd actually give it the list to work from.
screens.why2: 'The day's list' is what I call my call list every morning, so I get it on first hearing.
screens.why3: I can say whether I'd want to, but sending patient names and numbers to an outside tool isn't my call as an MA; my manager and the clinic's privacy rules decide that, so I'd be half guessing.
screens.why4: The four are distinct and in my words, but my real answer, 'yes, if my clinic approved it', is missing, and 'clearly worth it' doesn't cover that.
screens.why5: Only the idea card's own line about AI agents booking patients reaches me, and handing over the day's list is just what using it would mean.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and four short options plus 'you can't tell' are easy to hold when heard once.
screens.instead: To use Careforce, you'd hand the day's list to it. Would you do that, or not? Yes · Yes, if my clinic approved it · Yes, if it was clearly worth it · Probably not · No; escape: I can't tell
